stories.summary: Figure caption, Boateng Bismark James has been preaching on buses leaving Neoplan station since 2023 By Thomas Naadi BBC Africa ,Â Reporting from Accra Published 4 October 2026, 00:37 BST Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country. Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana. Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread. On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel. Photograph: Nordin Ćatić/St John's College, Cambridge Obituary John Iliffe obituary Pioneering historian who transformed the study of Africa by seeking out the testimonies of Africans When John Iliffe, who has died aged 87, wrote his book The African Poor: A History (1987), the continent was readily dismissed by many academics as a home of problems and poverty, with no intellectual depth. stories.title: Sudan: 'I Have Not Lost My Dreams' - Refugee Education Funding Cuts Threaten Millions
stories.summary: Sudan: 'I Have Not Lost My Dreams' - Refugee Education Funding Cuts Threaten Millions Asmaa Waguih/UNHCR Refugees wait to be registered at UNHCR is Cairo (file photo). 2 October 2026 UN News Service A teenage girl who fled war-torn Sudan for neighbouring Egypt and hopes to pursue a technology degree is an example of why countries must ensure that young refugees can continue to learn. "When we left Sudan, I was worried that my education would stop," said Jamila Mostafa, 19, one of the estimated 13.1 million refugee children of school age worldwide in 2025. Yet nearly half - 5.8 million - remain out of school as funding cuts threaten to roll back years of progress in educating children and adolescents forced to flee their homelands due to war, conflict, violence or persecution. A generation at risk Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn The warning comes in a new report by the UN refugee agency, UNHCR . "At a time of severe pressure on humanitarian and development financing, cuts to education risk reversing decades of collective investment and closing opportunities for a generation of young people," said UN High Commissioner for Refugees Barham Salih, a former refugee from Iraq. The transition to secondary education remains one of the biggest challenges for refugee children, according to the report. Only 32 per cent were enrolled in high school in 2025, compared to 65 per cent at the primary level.

stories.title: Kenya: City Hall Launches Day 2 of 'Operation Okoa Maisha' El Niño Emergency Simulation

stories.title: Trump is disappearing refugees into the hands of torturers – and rewarding them handsomely | Tutu Alicante and Uzra Zeya

stories.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 2, 2026
stories.summary: Africa: All of Africa Today - October 2, 2026 AllAfrica AllAfrica logo 2 October 2026 allAfrica.com By Melody Chironda Ethiopia, Eritrea Cut Diplomatic Ties as Conflict Escalates Ethiopia and Eritrea have severed diplomatic relations as renewed fighting in northern Ethiopia raises fears of a wider regional conflict. Ethiopia announced the closure of its embassy in Asmara and expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats, accusing them of posing a national security threat, prompting Eritrea to respond by cutting ties. The move follows worsening tensions over allegations that Eritrea is supporting armed groups fighting the Ethiopian government, which Asmara denies, as well as disagreements over Ethiopia's push for access to the Red Sea. Fighting between Ethiopian forces, the Tigray People's Liberation Front and allied groups has intensified across Tigray, Afar and Amhara. The African Union and United Nations have urged restraint and warned of growing risks to civilians and humanitarian operations.

stories.title: South Africa: Durban and Joburg Worst Hit By Water Outages
stories.summary: South Africa: Durban and Joburg Worst Hit By Water Outages 2 October 2026 GroundUp (Cape Town) These are the metros where long interruptions are most common Most South African households now have piped water. In 2025, 76% had a tap inside their home or on their property, according to Stats SA's General Household Survey. But in 2025, more than a third of households (about 38%) had water outages lasting two days or more. The eight metros did slightly better than the national average: 30% of their households reported long outages. Cape Town had the smallest share of households reporting long outages, at 8%. eThekwini had the largest, at 44%.

stories.title: Kenya: Warning - Heavy Rainfall Expected Across Kenya
stories.summary: Kenya: Heavy Rainfall Expected Across Kenya As Met Warns of Above-Average October Rains Capitol FM The heavy rainfall in Kenya (file photo). 2 October 2026 Capital FM (Nairobi) Nairobi — Kenya is expected to experience above-average rainfall in several parts of the country during October, with the Kenya Meteorological Department warning of heavy rainfall events in various areas. The weather agency said above-average rainfall, with higher probabilities, is expected in Kwale, Mombasa, Kilifi, Lamu and Mandera counties. Parts of Taita Taveta, Tana River, Garissa and Wajir are also expected to receive above-average rainfall during the month. The forecast indicates that Makueni, Kajiado, Machakos, Nairobi, Kiambu, Murang'a, Kirinyaga, Embu, Tharaka-Nithi, Meru, Isiolo, Nyandarua and Nyeri counties are also likely to receive above-average rainfall. stories.title: Alan Ferguson obituary
stories.summary: Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health View image in fullscreen Alan Ferguson, a fluent speaker of Swahili, worked for aid agencies in Kenya on family planning and public health Obituary Alan Ferguson obituary My brother, Alan Ferguson, who has died aged 79, was a Scotsman who began his working life as a geography lecturer at Nairobi University in Kenya , before working with aid agencies in that country. Alan joined the university in 1972, but left after a couple of years to teach in Britain at Cambridge University, and then in the US at NorthEastern University in Chicago. However, Kenya had got a hold on him, and he returned to work there, first for Amref , a Dutch organisation, and then GTZ, a German body, mainly in family planning and public health. Eventually he went freelance, helping various aid agencies with their work in Kenya, until a serious accident incapacitated him, forcing him to retire to Scotland. Born in Glasgow , Alan was the son of Bill, an analytical chemist, and Jessie (nee Moncrieff), a shorthand typist.

stories.title: Algeria introduces death penalty for arsonists after deadly wildfires
stories.summary: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images By Doug Faulkner Published 1 October 2026 Algeria has adopted a law imposing the death penalty on people convicted of arson of forests or fields after a series of deadly wildfires swept parts of the country. Members of the national assembly voted through the bill, which also made child abduction a capital offence, on Thursday. Capital punishment has been in the country's penal code for some offences, but no execution has been carried out since 1993. The official death toll from the blazes stands at 12, but independent news outlets believe the figure to be much higher. Algerian President Abdelmadjid Tebboune ordered the justice ministry to introduce the changes to the criminal law after more than 100 fires in the north-east of the country during an intense heatwave in northern Africa.

stories.title: Zimbabwe tycoon Wicknell Chivayo and wife killed in helicopter crash
stories.summary: Image source, Wicknell Chivayo/Instagram Image caption, Wicknell Chivayo was a prominent businessman known for his extravagant lifestyle By Wycliffe Muia Published 1 October 2026 Prominent Zimbabwean businessman Wicknell Chivayo and his wife have been killed in a helicopter crash that left six people dead, his family have confirmed. The helicopter came down in the Marondera rural area, about 70km (43 miles) east of the capital, Harare, on Wednesday evening. Police said all six people on board died. Family spokesperson Herbert Chivayo confirmed the deaths of the 43-year-old businessman and his wife Lucy Muteke to state broadcaster ZBC, saying the family was devastated by the tragedy. Chivayo was known for his lavish lifestyle, close ties to some African presidents and lucrative government contracts that had repeatedly attracted scrutiny.

stories.title: ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land
stories.summary: Much of the land taken during the colonial era has remained with the political elite and foreign companies occupying huge tea plantations. Photograph: Andrew H Brown View image in fullscreen Much of the land taken during the colonial era has remained with the political elite and foreign companies occupying huge tea plantations. Photograph: Andrew H Brown ‘They raped our country’: documentary follows Kenyans’ fight for restitution over stolen land Multinational tea companies still occupy ancestral highlands of communities displaced during British colonial era F or British colonialists, the fertile and cool uplands of central Kenya were the “White Highlands”, to be reserved exclusively for European settlers. Local communities were forced from the land, which was turned into plantations for tea and other crops. In recent decades, descendants of the displaced have fought to reclaim their ancestral land, some of which is now occupied by multinational tea companies and other large corporations.

Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Trump administration diverts human rights funds to push far-right agenda abroad Support such as for white Afrikaners and anti-communism reveals how US is redefining what qualifies as human rights With hours left before the funding expires, the Trump administration is pushing to direct more than $175m of the state department’s flagship human rights fund to a slate of awards that includes a huge $40m grant for an anti-communism fund, support for a group advancing white Afrikaner rights in South Africa, a campaign against Brazil’s supreme court and programs that would reward ideological allies in Europe who protect “western civilizational norms”. stories.title: Five EU states plan first deportation center in Africa for 2027
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NX1O Prospective migrants who arrived in Greece are taken into a migration hub Image: Sofia Kleftaki/DW Advertisement Deportation centers are legally contentious, expensive and the subject of political controversy: For years, Brussels has been grappling with the issue of establishing such centers outside the EU for rejected asylum seekers. Previous attempts have failed due to legal objections, but now, a "group of five" consisting of Greece , Germany , Austria , Denmark and the Netherlands believes it has overcome these hurdles . During an interview with the Greek television channel ANT1, Greece's Minister of Migration, Thanos Plevris, stated that the first of these so-called " return hubs " is scheduled to begin operations as early as the second half of 2027 — just in time for Greece to assume the EU Council Presidency. Plevris said Greece had chosen an African country but could not reveal its name yet. Diplomatic circles and media outlets close to the EU have repeatedly cited Rwanda or Uganda , but neither country has been confirmed as the location.

stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NRVf Senegal have refurbished some of their existing facilities rather than just building new ones Image: Cem Özdel/Anadolu/IMAGO Advertisement At the end of October 2026, the first ever Olympic event on African soil will take place as the Youth Olympics comes to Senegal . Around 2,700 young athletes are expected to compete across a total of 153 events in 25 sports, with many qualifying through the African Youth Games last year. "We were entrusted with hosting this event and that is why from Johannesburg to Nairobi, from Dakar to Djbouti, it is all of young Africa that is watching you and watching you with pride," Senegalese President Bassirou Diomaye Faye said at the arrival of the flame. The moment marks yet another step forward for global sport in Africa. In 2025, the first major road cycling event took place on the continent, and in September this year it was announced the first-ever World Athletics Championships would be held in Kenya in 2029. There are also on-going negotiations about Formula 1 returning.

stories.title: Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut
stories.summary: Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen. Photograph: Frida Marzouk View image in fullscreen Can she shape her own future? … Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as Al-Sit and Mihad Murtada as Nafisa in Cotton Queen. Photograph: Frida Marzouk Review Cotton Queen review – mystery, matriarchs and magic in pioneering Sudanese debut Suzannah Mirghani’s first feature contains a powerful performance by Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud as a village’s elder woman and tackles the long shadow of British imperialism and women’s rights ‘I decide my past,” says a village matriarch in this intriguingly political and poetic drama from Suzannah Mirghani, making her feature debut – and with it becoming the first Sudanese woman to direct a feature. (She was forced to cancel the original shoot in Sudan when war broke out in 2023 , moving production to Egypt.) It’s a film with things to say about the long shadow of the British empire, neocolonialism, women’s rights and female genital mutilation. But it mostly says it all without undermining its sense of mystery and shivers of magic realism. We’re in present day Sudan , where village elder Al-Sit (Rabha Mohamed Mahmoud) is an iron-willed woman not to be messed with.

stories.title: The journalist crowned king in Uganda after bitter succession dispute
stories.summary: Image source, Ngabo Amon/BBC By Basillioh Rukanga Â and Â Bella Twine ,Â BBC Focus on Africa Published 29 September 2026 Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma has been crowned king of Uganda's Tooro kingdom. The new monarch has long been a familiar face in the East African nation, where for many he was known not as the heir to the throne, but as a storyteller: a long-serving anchor and editor at the state broadcaster. But the 56-year-old - now King Edward Rukidi Kijanangoma Nyabongo I - has become the subject of media attention himself as his rise to the Tooro throne sparked controversy and widespread reactions beyond the country. Tooro is one of Uganda's four main officially recognised historical kingdoms. For the last 31 years, it had been headed by King Oyo Nyimba Kabamba Iguru Rukidi IV, who was once known as a "boy king", after ascending to the throne as an infant.

stories.title: Ethiopia: No regard for civilians as fighting in Tigray continues
stories.summary: https://p.dw.com/p/5NQMb Prices in Tigrayan towns like Mekelle have surged since the onset of the fighting Image: REUTERS Advertisement As fighting keeps spreading across northern Ethiopia , civilians find themselves caught in the crossfire between opposing forces. Little information is emerging from the affected area as the internet and other communication services remain largely disrupted . However, DW managed to speak to eyewitnesses whose accounts point to a growing toll on civilians. A 22-year-old woman from the small town of Selenwuha told DW that her relatives were sheltering at home when heavy weaponry shelling struck their residences. "I have lost six family members," she said. "Those who survived the attack, including the wounded, are currently confined to their homes. "They have no access to medical facilities or vehicles, and the nearest treatment center is far away." Strategic town of Alamata reported taken by ENDF According to local residents, several violent incidents took place in recent days, especially in the border region between the Tigray and Amhara regions, with multiple further reports of civilians being killed by artillery fire. The overall strategic situation on the ground meanwhile remains difficult to assess, with both rebel and federal forces reportedly making advances in different areas .

stories.summary: Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety Son of Zambian bishop detained in post-election raid fears for his father's safety Close The son of detained Zambian opposition politician Bishop Trevor Mwamba has told the BBC he is concerned for his father's safety after the former Bishop of Botswana was detained along with 10 other opposition figures by authorities. Eno Mwamba said his father, who is leader of the United National Independence Party, has been charged with treason following President Hakainde Hichilema's disputed election victory. The opposition politicians have been held since a raid by security forces on 14 August. Opposition leader Brian Mundubile, head of the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), had gone into hiding after disputing the election result, but has since also been detained by the authorities. The government accuses the opposition of planning an armed insurgency and have charged the detained politicians with treason.

Photograph: Aina Zo Raberanto/The Guardian Murdered for their eyes: people with albinism living in terror in Madagascar The country is struggling to address a rise in attacks, with a record 13 people – mostly children – killed this year for body parts, which some believe can bring good fortune Not long after midnight in late May this year, three men barged through the door of the small room where Nicole Soalala lived with her family on the outskirts of Toliara, a coastal city in the south of Madagascar . Her husband got up to ask what they wanted, but they attacked him with a piece of wood and an axe. Soalala, 32, grabbed her youngest child, Landricia – an 18-month-old girl with albinism – and hoisted her on to her back, holding her there with a piece of fabric she started to wrap around herself.

stories.title: Twelve women have been killed in one part of South Africa since July. Here's what we know so far
stories.summary: Image source, AFP via Getty Images Image caption, The discovery of 12 bodies in an area east of Johannesburg has sparked alarm in South Africa By Khanyisile Ngcobo Reporting from Johannesburg Published 28 September 2026 Police in South Africa have confirmed the discovery of the bodies of three more women in an area east of Johannesburg, bringing the total number of bodies found there to 12 in just two months. The latest bodies were found in Ekurhuleni between Saturday and Monday morning, according to local police. Police have made arrests in three of the cases, which do not appear to be related to the others. Nevertheless, police have said they cannot rule out the possibility of a serial killer. The discoveries have caused widespread alarm in Ekurhuleni, particularly around Kempton Park, and come against the backdrop of longstanding concerns about high levels of violence against women in South Africa.

An Iranian dissident to Central African Republic . A Cameroonian to Equatorial Guinea. This is the face of the Trump administration’s deportations policy since 2025 – striking deals with 35 countries, and sending up to 25,000 migrants in the US across the world, often to places they have no connection to at all. The South African police service said on Sunday that 17 people were killed on Saturday night when eight suspects armed with AK-47 assault rifles and pistols opened fire at a bar in Wedela township, about 50 miles south-west of central Johannesburg. At least 15 other people sustained gunshot injuries in that attack, police said.
